blocks.text: The masters of the Jews rightly assert that the name of the bird דוכיפת dukiphath is a compound. But the reason for the compounding escapes them. If we believe Pagninus, R. Selomo in his Commentary explains it as the wild cock, δίλοφον [dilophon], that is, having a double crest; and he holds that it is called דוכיפת dukiphath from its double crest, as though having דוכיפות dukephoth, that is (he says), two crests. Compounds of this kind occur not infrequently in the writings of the Rabbis. Thus the cave of Machpelah, or the double cave, is called by them דיוטרון, as if double cavern, a word fused from δύο [dyo] and ἄντρον [antron]. The first man is דיופרצוף, διπρόσωπος [diprosōpos], as though God had created him two-faced. A siphon is דיופי, as though it had two mouths. A tree bearing twice a year is דיופרא, as if δίφορος [diphoros]. A double bag is דיוסקיא, as if δίσακκος [disakkos], like the French bissac and besace. The two magistrates governing a city, or consuls, are דיופולין, from δύο [dyo] and πόλις [polis]. A two-edged sword is דיוסטר, because of its two sides; for to them סטר is side. An image copied from another is דיוקון, from δύο [dyo] and εἰκών [eikōn]. Two columns are דיומדין, from דיו and עומדין. And דיוזגי, δίζυγος [dizygos], bijugus [two-yoked]. And דוכסוסטוס, as if δύξυστος [dyxystos], scraped twice: just as παλίμψηστος [palimpsēstos] is a certain kind of parchment, scraped and polished either twice or on both sides. Accordingly, as though the words of the Prophets admitted similar compounds, Joseph Kimchi, the father of David, on Psalm 50, verse 20, contends that the word דופי dophi, that is, reproach, censure, is compounded of דו do, two, and פי pi or phi, mouth; because a slanderer speaks one way in your presence and another in your absence, as though he [col. 344] had two mouths. It is quite absurd that a word used by David should be taken for half-Latin, or at least half-Greek. But it is far more absurd in the case of Moses, to whom belongs the word דוכיפת dukiphath that we are dealing with. In truth, to tell the matter as it is, R. Selomo does not write what Pagninus attributes to him, that the bird דוכיפת dukiphath takes its name from דוכפות du-kephoth, or two crests. For there is no bird that is δίλοφος [dilophos]. And a crest in Hebrew is not called כיפה kepha or כיפת kephath, but כרבלה kirbela, as the Bretons say cribel. Finally, the words of Solomon cited by Pagninus mean something quite different: ולמה נקרא שמו דוכיפת שהודו כפות וזו היא כרבלתו. They are to be rendered thus: And why is its name called dukiphath? Because its eminence is bound, that is, its crest. For הוד hod means splendour, dignity, majesty, eminence. And the verb כפת kephath in Chaldee is to bind and to tie. He means, then, that from the two words הודו כפות hodo kaphuth, that is, its eminence (or crest) is bound (supply to its head), dukiphath was formed by aphaeresis, because it is the name of a crested bird. Nor is this so much R. Selomo's as the Talmudists', in Chullin ch. 3, fol. 63a, where R. Judah says that the דוכיפת dukiphath is so called שהודו כפות, because it has its eminence bound. And [III, 108] the Gloss in the margin: כרבלתו עבה ורומה כמו שכפולה לתוך הראש וכפותה שם, Its crest is thick, and as it were tied in the middle of the head and bound there. For in place of שכפולה, which means doubled, one must read שכבולה, that is, tied, as the sense shows, together with the synonymous word כפותה that follows. There is a similar error in the Aruch in these words: דוכיפת זה שהודו כפוף. For one must read כפות, as in the Talmud and Selomo, not כפוף. Meanwhile this derivation is not much better than the former. For although הוד hod signifies the ὑπεροχὴν [hyperochēn] and eminence of splendour, strength, glory, dignity and majesty, it is nowhere taken for a crest. Nor would a crested bird rightly be said to have its crest bound, since in crested birds the crest is innate, not bound on. It is clear, therefore, that this ἔτυμον [etymon] is very forced and wrung out as if on the rack.
